headline_short: Cloud Earnings Outrun a Divided Fed
preheader: Three Fed officials voted to hike. The 30-year mortgage hit 6.66%. Gas is up 97 cents in a year. And the best 1-year CDs at 4.40% suddenly look durable.

lead.headline: Three Fed officials voted to raise rates this week - the first triple dissent toward a hike this cycle - and the bond market listened. The 10-year Treasury ended the week at 4.75% and the 30-year mortgage at 6.66%, even after a soft GDP print and the first monthly decline in consumer prices since April 2020.
lead.context: Stocks rallied anyway on the strength of the cloud earnings below. The bigger takeaway: cheap money is not coming back on the schedule markets assumed a month ago, and that changes the math for savers and borrowers alike.
lead.link_text: Read what a divided Fed means for rates, CDs, and mortgages

bullets.bold: Big Tech split into two tiers.
bullets.rest: Microsoft rose 15% on Azure's 43% growth and Amazon crossed $200B in quarterly revenue with AWS up 37% - while Meta fell 9% on weak guidance and Apple guided below consensus on rising memory costs.

bullets.bold: The week's gain hides a narrow market.
bullets.rest: The S&P 500 added 1.0% and the Nasdaq 1.6%, but the Russell 2000 sat flat - small caps got no invitation to the cloud rally. The VIX fell to 16.

bullets.bold: Gas crossed $4.10 nationally, up 97 cents from a year ago.
bullets.rest: California is paying $5.49 while the Gulf Coast pays $3.69 - the widest practical spread in the country.

bullets.bold: Foreclosure starts are up 18% year over year, and FHA delinquency hit 11.88%.
bullets.rest: Distress is building at the edges of the housing market even as the median price set a record $440,600 - two markets wearing one average.

bullets.bold: The best 1-year CDs at 4.40% now look durable rather than fleeting.
bullets.rest: The national average bank still pays 1.68% on the same insured product - a 2.6x gap that a phone call closes.
